newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl gets breather in German budget feud.
newsitem.headline: Kohl gets breather in German budget feud.

text.p: The latest truce in Bonn's budget feud could be only a short breather before Chancellor Helmut Kohl plunges into another round of squabbling over cuts and reforms to slim down Germany's welfare state.

Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU/CSU) and their liberal Free Democrat (FDP) coalition partners agreed on the main lines of the 1997 budget late on Sunday evening after a tense week that included a rare threat from the veteran chancellor to resign.

The new draft budget, three billion marks ($2 billion) slimmer after the latest wave of belt-tightening among the fractious cabinet ministers, met the primary goal of ensuring Germany respected the strict Maastricht limits on new government borrowing.

But the 14-year coalition pulled off this trick only by putting off until December the most explosive dispute in the coalition, the FDP's demand that the hated "solidarity tax" for east Germany be reduced by two percentage points in 1998.

That means the dispute should flare up again next month, just when the government plans to start debating a far more comprehensive tax reform expected to draw howls of protest from vested interests set to lose their privileges.

"The government is stumbling along from one budget shortfall to the next," said Klaus-Peter Schoeppner of the Emnid opinion polling group. "Its message is that we have to save even more, but nobody knows how."
"There can be no talk about an end to the budget misery," the Handelsblatt daily commented. "(Finance Minister Theo Waigel) has not won anything more than just a breather."

The business daily noted with concern that Waigel trimmed his overall 1997 budget down to 440 billion marks with several one-off savings like delaying a planned tax cut, early sales of some government real estate and some privatisation revenues.
His estimates for unemployment support payments, which ballooned this year due to rising jobless figures, were shaky since they were based on an estimated 2.5 percent economic growth rate, it added.
"Even if Waigel makes it through the coming months, the hole-plugging will start all over again in the early summer of 1997 when the 1998 budget is drafted," Handelsblatt wrote.
The strains of the budget feud have increasingly poisoned the atmosphere between the three coalition parties, Kohl's CDU, its CSU sister party in Bavaria and the small FDP.
Juergen Moellemann, the former economics minister, lashed out at Kohl on Sunday for not agreeing to FDP demands for more tax cuts, saying: "Kohl should keep his paws off the FDP."
Waigel ridiculed Moellemann in a television interview and waved a red flag at the FDP by talking at a weekend meeting of his CSU about possible new taxes.
A leading Christian Democrat, Heiner Geissler, remarked: "The FDP, with its six or seven percent of the vote, has to finally realise it is not the centre of the world."
Despite the tensions, coalition leaders repeat like a soothing mantra that they have no alternative but to continue with the present alliance into the 1998 general election.
The latest Emnid poll showed that 63 percent of those queried were dissatisfied with the government's performance -- but 74 percent expected Kohl's coalition to soldier on.
The polls showed the government and a potential alliance of the opposition SPD and Greens running neck-and-neck with both winning 45 percent support.
But the left-leaning SPD, the main opposition party, still presents little credible alternative to the CDU in Bonn.

The party also suffered an embarrassing defeat on Sunday when the Greens candidate for mayor in Stuttgart scored a whopping 39 percent of the vote while two Social Democrats running in the same race totalled barely 17 percent together.
The winner, though, was the CDU candidate with 43 percent.
